source_reviews.independent_solution: For a nondegenerate right circular cone: (1) an axial section is an isosceles triangle with equal slants and base a diameter; (2) an interior plane parallel to the base gives a disk (called a circle in the school section convention); (3) a cutting plane through the apex gives an isosceles triangle because both end-to-apex generators have the same length. The wording 'through the apex' alone also permits a supporting plane with only one generator as the intersection, or an exterior-to-the-cone plane with only the apex. A base-parallel plane at the apex gives a point. Thus the usual triangle/circle statements require genuine nondegenerate cuts; do not silently turn 'every plane through the apex' into 'every triangle'. Conditions: Positive radius and height; genuine cuts for the familiar shapes. Drawing/proof recognition loses independent construction but is not inherently a failed mathematical task.

coverage.evidence: One unified unit retains axial, interior parallel and positive-chord apex shapes and explicitly tests supporting-plane degeneration. Author coverage acknowledges free classification proof and drawing are not observed; no shape task is omitted.

source_reviews.independent_solution: No central symmetry: the unique apex would have to map to itself, forcing the center to be the apex, but reflecting any base point through it leaves the solid. Exactly one spatial symmetry/rotation axis, the apex-to-base-center line; infinitely many symmetry planes, precisely all planes through this line. A horizontal plane swaps an apex and a disk and is not a symmetry plane. Neither a generator nor a base diameter is a spatial symmetry axis. Conditions: Finite nondegenerate right circular cone, not a double cone. Spatial axis symmetry is not the count of symmetry axes of the base circle.

coverage.evidence: The center/one-axis/infinitely-many-planes tuple covers both source subparts. Omitted independent proofs are explicitly recorded; base-circle axis counts are not substituted for spatial symmetry.

source_reviews.independent_solution: (1) Half the axial section is a right triangle, r=l*sin(phi/2), h=l*cos(phi/2), so base area is pi*l^2*sin(phi/2)^2. (2) r=sqrt(Q/pi), h=sqrt(l^2-Q/pi), and axial triangle area is (2r)*h/2 = sqrt((Q/pi)*(l^2-Q/pi)). Conditions: l>0, 0<phi<pi; for (2), 0<Q<pi*l^2. Boundary values describe degenerate solids, not ordinary cones.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Let apex S project to base center O, and let M be the foot from O on the trace chord line AB. h=R*tan(alpha). The angle between section and base is phi, so OM=d=h*cot(phi), SM=h/sin(phi), and half chord AM=sqrt(R^2-d^2). The triangular section area is AM*SM = R^2*tan(alpha)*sqrt(1-tan(alpha)^2*cot(phi)^2)/sin(phi). Equivalent form h*sqrt(R^2-h^2*cot(phi)^2)/sin(phi). At phi=pi/2 the section is axial and area is R*h. At phi=alpha it is tangent/one generator and area 0. For 0<phi<alpha no positive-area cut exists. This is a plane/base dihedral angle, not the angle between two generators. Conditions: R>0, 0<alpha<pi/2; nondegenerate triangular section alpha<phi<=pi/2. Tangency phi=alpha must not be claimed to produce a nondegenerate triangle.
